passage: Samir read the plan Devika had pinned on the dairy cooperative's noticeboard: buy the chilling tank, install it, start collecting milk by the fifteenth. Three neat boxes, two weeks. He had run the cooperative's works for many years and he could almost hear what the boxes left out. He didn't say it was wrong. He asked, “Who signs off the site before the tank comes?” Devika went quiet. On a fresh sheet they drew the hidden boxes: the electricity board's approval, a water test, the fitter's schedule, three days of trial running. Two weeks on the sheet turned into six, and Devika looked relieved, not defeated, to see the real dates.

qa.q: How long did Devika's plan say the work would take?
qa.a: Devika's plan showed two weeks, with three boxes: buy the tank, install it and start collecting milk.

qa.q: What did Samir think when he read Devika's neat three-box plan?
qa.a: Samir suspected the plan was missing steps, since Samir could almost hear what the boxes left out, and felt gently concerned rather than critical.

qa.q: What could Devika do the next time a plan is made?
qa.a: Ask, for each visible job, who has to approve it, what must be tested and what has to be waited for, and put those hidden steps on the sheet from the start.

qa.q: How might Devika feel when the plan grows from two weeks to six?
qa.a: Devika may feel a little surprised at first, but relief grows because the real dates protect the work from surprises.

grounding: An experienced person notices that a newer person's plan leaves out approvals, testing and waiting time.

passage: Olga showed Mei the plan for the client's brochure at the studio in Melbourne: design on Monday and Tuesday, print on Wednesday, deliver on Thursday. It was tidy, colour-coded and very confident. Mei nodded, then tapped the space between the boxes. “Where's the client's approval round? Where's the proof check?” she asked. Olga blinked. “And the printer has a queue, doesn't it?” Mei said. They rebuilt the week together on the whiteboard, adding a day for the client to reply, a day for corrections, two days of print queue. Thursday delivery became the following Wednesday, and Olga wrote the new date in a fresh marker, a little pink in the face.

qa.q: Which day did Olga's plan say the brochure would be delivered?
qa.a: Olga's plan said the brochure would be delivered on Thursday.

qa.q: Why did Mei tap the space between the boxes?
qa.a: Mei felt concerned but kind: she noticed the plan skipped the connecting work, such as the client's approval and the proof check, and wanted Olga to see the gap without being blamed.

qa.q: What did the new plan add, and what did it change?
qa.a: It added a client approval day, a corrections day and two days of print queue, so Thursday delivery moved to the following Wednesday.

qa.q: How might Olga be feeling as the date is rewritten?
qa.a: Olga is likely a bit embarrassed, shown by turning pink, but also learning that the hidden steps are what usually eat the schedule.

grounding: An experienced person notices that a newer person's plan leaves out approval, checking and waiting steps.

passage: The site office of the metro project smelled of tea and printer ink. Abhinav, eight years into the job, leaned over Nitin's laptop. Nitin had built his first schedule for the station's drainage work: survey, design, dig, lay pipes, done in six weeks. Neat bars, nothing overlapping. Abhinav felt a familiar tug of recognition; his own first schedule had looked exactly like this. "Where's the approval from the city engineer?" he asked. Nitin blinked. "And pressure testing? And the week we'll wait for pipe delivery?" Nitin's ears went red. Abhinav pulled up a chair. "Add them in, then we'll see what six weeks really means." The new chart said ten.

qa.q: How many weeks did Nitin's first schedule show?
qa.a: Nitin's first schedule showed six weeks.

qa.q: What was Abhinav feeling as he looked at Nitin's schedule?
qa.a: He felt a familiar, almost fond recognition, because his own first schedule had looked exactly like this.

qa.q: How did Abhinav handle the gaps, and why did it work?
qa.a: He asked questions about approval, testing and delivery waits instead of lecturing, then sat with Nitin to add them, which turned six weeks into an honest ten.

qa.q: What is it like for Nitin when Abhinav points out the missing steps?
qa.a: Nitin feels embarrassed, his ears going red, but he also gets a far more realistic plan from someone who once made the same mistake.

grounding: A senior colleague notices that a junior's schedule leaves out approvals, testing and waiting time.

passage:
Subject: Your launch plan, a few thoughts

Hi Hafsa,

I read your plan for the new billing page last night. The design and coding steps are clear, and your estimate for them looks fair. I noticed something I missed too when I started: the plan has no room for sign-off from legal, no time for the testing team, and no gap for the two-day wait while the security team reviews it. In my experience those in-between steps take as long as the build itself.

Could we sit tomorrow at eleven and add them? I think the date will move by about two weeks, and it's better we say so now.

Ritu

qa.q: What three missing steps did Ritu notice in the plan?
qa.a: The plan had no room for sign-off from legal, no time for the testing team and no gap for the two-day security review wait.

qa.q: How does Ritu seem to feel about pointing out the gaps?
qa.a: Ritu seems kind and a little protective, not critical, admitting to having missed the same steps when starting out.

qa.q: What would you advise Hafsa to do at the eleven o'clock meeting?
qa.a: Hafsa could list every hand-off and wait with Ritu, then share the corrected date early rather than defending the first one.

qa.q: How might Hafsa feel reading the email?
qa.a: Hafsa may feel a sting of embarrassment at first, then relief that the problem was caught before the date was promised.

grounding: A senior colleague's email flags that a junior's plan leaves out approvals, testing and waiting time.

passage: You asked what mentoring is really like. I'm Tenzin, and I'll give you one afternoon. Anjali, our new analyst, brought me her plan for the donor report. Collect data, analyse, write, send. Two weeks. She was so proud, and honestly, it was tidy. But I felt a little knot, because I'd seen this before. I asked, "Who has to approve the numbers?" Finance. "How long do they take?" She didn't know. Four days, usually. Then the director reads it. Then the designer. Then corrections. We sat and wrote them all in. Two weeks became four. She looked deflated. A month later she thanked me, because the report went out on time.

qa.q: Who has to approve the numbers in Anjali's report?
qa.a: Finance has to approve the numbers.

qa.q: What did Tenzin feel when first seeing Anjali's tidy plan?
qa.a: Tenzin felt a little knot of worry, recognising the pattern of a beginner leaving out the in-between steps.

qa.q: Which approach from Tenzin helped, and why?
qa.a: Asking simple questions about who approves and how long it takes let Anjali find the missing steps herself, so two weeks honestly became four.

qa.q: How did Anjali react at first, and how did that change?
qa.a: Anjali looked deflated when the plan doubled, but a month later felt grateful because the report went out on time.

grounding: A senior colleague notices a junior's plan omits approvals and waiting and helps add them in.

passage:
I've been at the company six years, and I sit across from Akash, who joined in January. Last week he was asked to set up the new visitor ID cards for our office.
On Monday he showed me his plan on a single sheet: order blank cards Monday, print Tuesday, go live Wednesday. He looked pleased. It was neat.
I asked, "Who has to approve the card design?" He blinked. Security has to sign off, and they meet on Thursdays. I asked about testing the card printer; it hadn't been used since last year. And the blank cards come from a supplier in another city: four working days, minimum.
He went quiet and started writing in the margin. By the end, Wednesday had become the Wednesday after next.
I'm Jaya, by the way, and I did the same thing in my first year with a canteen contract. Nobody plans the waiting. It's always the waiting.

qa.q: On which day does the security team meet?
qa.a: They meet on Thursdays.

qa.q: How does Jaya seem to feel watching Akash's plan change?
qa.a: Jaya seems sympathetic rather than critical, remembering making the same mistake with a canteen contract.

qa.q: What should Akash add to future plans?
qa.a: Approvals, testing and waiting times, such as security sign-off, printer checks and supplier delivery, since those steps eat the schedule.

qa.q: How might Akash have felt as Wednesday became the Wednesday after next?
qa.a: Akash probably felt deflated and a little embarrassed, having been pleased with a neat plan that missed the hidden steps.

grounding: An observer senior sees a junior's plan leave out approvals, testing and waiting time, the connecting steps that usually eat the schedule.
